title: Photonic Cluster State Generation from a Quantum Dot Emitting in the Telecom C-band
authors: Giora Peniakov, Reza Hekmati, Johannes Michl, Mohamed Helal, Moritz Meinecke, Jochen Kaupp, Yorick Reum, Martin Kamp, Monika Emmerling, Andreas Theo Pfenning, Sven Hoefling, Tobias Huber-Loyola
abstract: Photonic cluster states are a key resource for photonic quantum information processing. So far, deterministic generation of these states has been limited to the near-infrared wavelength range. To achieve quantum advantage in communication while maintaining compatibility with silicon photonics, operation in the telecom wavelength range is required. In this work, we demonstrate deterministic cluster state generation directly in the telecom C-band. This is achieved through repetitive excitation of a hole spin confined in an indium-arsenide quantum dot subjected to an external magnetic field. We characterize the quantum process that generates the cluster state by measuring its process map, obtaining a fidelity of $\mathrm{F} = 0.71 \pm 0.01$ to the ideal case. As part of this characterization, we observe spin--photon polarization entanglement with a negativity of $\mathrm{N} = 0.27 \pm 0.02$. The emitted photons exhibit indistinguishability of at least 83%, demonstrating the potential for future fusion gates necessary for photonic cluster state generation beyond linear connectivity.
summary: The paper reports the deterministic generation of photonic cluster states in the telecom C-band using an InAs quantum dot. By leveraging hole spin qubits and characterizing the underlying process map, the authors demonstrated entanglement and achieved a three-qubit state fidelity of 0.71. This work is significant because it enables scalable quantum information processing compatible with existing optical fiber infrastructure.
main_problem: The primary goal is to deterministically generate photonic cluster states directly within the telecom C-band, which is crucial for quantum communication compatibility with existing fiber infrastructure.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated deterministic generation of a three-qubit cluster state in the telecom C-band using an InAs quantum dot system. They achieved a process map fidelity of 0.71 and high photon indistinguishability ($\geq 83\%$).
method: Cluster state generation is realized by implementing a Circuit Building Block (CBB) sequence involving controlled-NOT gates and single-qubit rotations, all characterized via quantum process tomography.
model_or_system: The system uses an Indium-arsenide ($	ext{InAs}$) quantum dot embedded in a microcavity. Qubit encoding is achieved using the hole spin state, while photonic entanglement is generated through optical transitions to the positive trion ($	ext{X}^+$) at 1549 nm.
key_observables: Cluster state fidelity ($\mathcal{F} = 0.71 \pm 0.01$), spin–photon polarization entanglement negativity ($\mathcal{N} = 0.27 \pm 0.02$), and photon indistinguishability ($V_{HOM} \geq 0.83$).
important_parameters: The process operates at an $80 	ext{ MHz}$ repetition rate, utilizing a hole-spin coherence time ($T_2^*$) of $15.9 \pm 1.7 	ext{ ns}$.
main_assumptions: The characterization assumes that the fidelity can be extrapolated for larger cluster states by concatenating the CBB result multiple times.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the microcavity setup, the PL spectrum showing the $	ext{X}^+$ transition, and detailed circuit diagrams outlining the sequence of CNOT and single-qubit gates used to build the cluster state.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical platform (QD in a cavity), outlines the protocol based on CBBs derived from spin/photon interactions, presents characterization results via process tomography and entanglement measurements, and concludes with the demonstration of multi-qubit cluster state generation.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a major bottleneck in quantum networking by achieving high-fidelity photonic resource generation at telecom wavelengths using solid-state emitters, bridging fundamental physics research with practical quantum technology requirements.
